Jay Leno Drives the Corvette That Fooled Millions as a Ferrari on Miami Vice
14 photos
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube
The Ferrari that Sonny Crockett, played by Don Johnson, drove during the first two seasons of Miami Vice was actually a replica of a 1972 Ferrari Daytona Spyder built on the chassis of a C3 Chevrolet Corvette. The man who built it has just parked it in Jay Leno's Garage.
Back in the early 1980s, kit car builder Tom McBurnie visited Newport Beach exotic car dealer Al Mardikian to discuss building Shelby Cobra replicas. After Mardikian passed on his price, McBurnie spotted a white 1972 Ferrari Daytona Spyder sitting in the showroom on consignment.
He quietly borrowed the car for a year to pull fiberglass molds from its body without the owner ever finding out. Then, he spent months reshaping the proportions to fit the C3 Chevy Corvette chassis.
After Mardikian displayed a finished replica at the Balboa Bay Club, word reached Miami Vice creator Michael Mann, who immediately wanted it as Sonny Crockett’s car. So Tom McBurnie's replica, a black fiberglass conversion, stood in for an authentic Daytona Spyder.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Real Ferrari Daytonas were extremely rare and expensive in the 1980s. Besides, Ferrari North America turned down Miami Vice because of a strict company policy against loaning or donating cars for television productions.
The production team went for the replica built on the third-generation Corvette chassis, with the first show cars using 1976 and 1981 models. Adapting the shape of the Ferrari Daytona to the chassis of the C3 Corvette required major bodywork changes, including a fiberglass body with a black plexiglass nose section.
Tom McBurnie resorted to that technical solution because the real Daytona had a 94.5-inch (2,400-millimeter) wheelbase versus the 98 inches (2,489 millimeters) that the C3 Corvette sat on, along with narrower doors and a narrower windshield.
The cabin of the Corvette was restyled to resemble that of a Ferrari. It was upgraded with tan Connolly leather upholstery and black Wilton wool carpeting, though it retained high-backed Corvette seats rather than the real Daytona’s lower seats with separate headrests.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Visible door handles with integrated keyholes held their ground, while the Daytonas had hidden handles and separate door locks. The rear bodywork was far flatter than the original sloping rear end of the authentic Ferrari.
All the time, Tom kept in touch with the stunt men of the TV series. The stunt team added a second brake pedal in the driver’s footwell, which controlled only the rear brakes, allowing stunt drivers to lock up the rear wheels on command while keeping the front wheels free to steer.
To keep the illusion alive on screen, the Miami Vice sound editors stripped out the Corvette's raw production audio during driving scenes and replaced it with post-production dubs of a genuine Ferrari V12.
For Season 2, McBurnie’s replicas were further refined. They came with a smoother front end, tinted headlight covers, repositioned Ferrari badges, and matching windshield trim. However, no matter how hard they tried, Ferrari didn't like it.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Ferrari pushed back against the replica cars in the series and took legal action over trademark infringement and look-alikes. The Italian house eventually offered to supply two 1986 Ferrari Testarossas on the condition that the fake Daytonas be retired.
The producers agreed and wrote the swap into the series. In the Season 3 premiere, When Irish Eyes Are Crying, Sonny Crockett’s black Daytona was destroyed by a Stinger missile, clearing the way for a white Testarossa to become his new signature ride. The car wasn’t really destroyed. It now sits, looking shiny and new, in Jay Leno's Garage as a guest.
This is what he takes for a spin around Los Angeles to check out how the 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) V8 behaves years after its stint in Miami. It has 180 horsepower (182 metric horsepower) on tap, but no Miami Vice clothes and soundtrack available. Still, with Tom in the passenger seat, they look like retired undercover detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo "Rico" Tubbs.
A third Daytona replica was in the making by custom car fabricator and kit-car builder Carl Roberts, but the project was dropped when the Testarossa deal went through. One of the replicas in the TV series went to a private collector, while the stunt car later appeared in the 1989 film Speed Zone and was restored for display at the Volo Auto Museum.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Now, one of those cars is parked in Jay Leno ’s Garage. It was brought there by the man who built it. Tom McBurnie tells the story of the Ferrari-wannabe Corvette. He also recalls how Ferrari did everything they could to put him out of business.
Miami Vice turned McBurnie's Daytona Spyder into a sensation, and his business simply exploded from a tiny operation with part-time employees into a 55-person affair, selling dozens of turnkey cars and hundreds of body kits. He would not sell Ferrari badges, but owners of the conversion cars bought the prancing horse logos themselves and slapped them onto the front of their vehicles.
This was seen by Ferrari as a major threat to its brand exclusivity, and they went after him in every way possible. They claimed ownership of the model’s shape and sued McBurnie Coachcraft in federal court under the Lanham Act for infringing its trade dress, arguing that the Daytona Spyder's silhouette was so "unique and distinctive" that copying it alone violated Ferrari's intellectual property.
McBurnie argued his replicas were like art lithographs that only boosted the real Daytona's fame and value. And he wasn't wrong. Real Ferrari Daytona prices on the used car market jumped from roughly $100,000 - $150,000 before Miami Vice to over $1.5 million in a couple of years.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Michael Mann testified in McBurnie’s favor, making clear that Miami Vice specifically wanted the replica for production practicality and never confused it with a factory Ferrari. Still, McBurnie had to pay his own attorneys, depositions, and court costs over several years of fighting Ferrari in federal court, costing him a total of $640,000.
On April 28, 1989, a fire devastated Tom McBurnie's shop in Santee, California, severely damaging the building and destroying multiple vehicles inside. A month later, a federal court injunction legally banned him from making Daytona replicas, which, combined with the legal bills and the fire, ended McBurnie Coachcraft’s story and put Tom McBurnie out of business.
